options: Every time the optimizer would have benefited from an index that doesn't currently exist, including the columns it needed
The exact indexes that were dropped in the last 24 hours
Only indexes on system tables
Indexes that have already been created but are fragmented
questions.explain: equality_columns and included_columns tell you what to lead with and what to include when creating the suggested index.

questions.q: Why should avg_user_impact from the missing-index DMVs be treated as a hint rather than a guarantee?
options: It's the optimizer's own estimate of improvement, and should be verified against a real execution plan before and after creating the index
It is always exactly accurate and never needs verification
It only applies to clustered indexes
It measures disk space, not query performance
questions.explain: This lesson stresses verifying the actual effect with Lesson 45's execution-plan reading skills before trusting the estimate.

questions.q: What makes two nonclustered indexes 'duplicate candidates'?
options: They share the same leading (first) key column, even if their included columns differ
They are on the same table but have completely different leading columns
One is clustered and the other is nonclustered
They were both created in the same calendar year
questions.explain: Every index costs write overhead on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, so redundant leading columns are wasted maintenance cost.

questions.q: An index shows zero user_seeks, zero user_scans, and zero user_lookups in sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats, but a high user_updates count. What does that mean?
options: The index is pure overhead -- absorbing write cost on every table change while returning zero query benefit
The index is being used very efficiently
The index has been corrupted and must be rebuilt immediately
The table has no data in it
questions.explain: It's a strong candidate to drop, after confirming with a representative time window rather than checking right after a restart.

questions.q: Why can't you conclude an index has 'never been used' just because sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats currently shows zero usage?
options: The DMV's counters reset on every SQL Server service restart, so zero usage might just mean zero usage since the last restart
The DMV only tracks usage for clustered indexes
The DMV is always empty by design
Usage stats can only be viewed by a server administrator, never a DBA
questions.explain: This lesson calls this out explicitly as a caveat -- check over a representative window, not right after a failover or restart.
